claims.text: The specialized machine-learning model is trained on an extensive experimental dataset of HEAs with measured phonon thermal conductivity.
The model can accurately identify HEAs with intrinsically low phonon thermal conductivity.
Nonlinear machine-learning models can capture useful relationships among HEA descriptors.
Atomic-size mismatch, mixing entropy, and mixing enthalpy directly encode the phonon-scattering behavior controlling HEA lattice thermal conductivity.
The specialized model will outperform conventional empirical or physics-based thermal-conductivity models.
Conventional empirical or physics-based models do not fully account for nonlinear interactions among alloy descriptors.
Compositional and atomic disorder in single-phase HEAs promotes phonon scattering.
Point defects and atomic-scale disorder enhance phonon scattering and reduce phonon relaxation times.
Shorter phonon relaxation times lead to lower lattice thermal conductivity.
Nanostructuring increases boundary scattering of phonons.
Alloying introduces point-defect scattering that is particularly effective for high-frequency phonons.
Anharmonic lattice vibrations produce phonon-phonon scattering that contributes to low lattice thermal conductivity.
The model can infer boundary, point-defect, and anharmonic scattering mechanisms by weighting and combining the selected descriptors.
Measured phonon thermal conductivities of model-selected HEAs will be approximately 10% or more below values predicted by conventional methods.
Model accuracy will be limited to compositions, phases, and processing histories similar to those represented in its training data.
The model may not generalize reliably to non-HEAs, highly ordered alloys, or substantially different processing histories.
HEA phase-prediction studies demonstrate that nonlinear machine-learning models can reach approximately 86% classification accuracy.
The expected magnitude of improvement can vary with dataset quality, descriptor selection, and experimental uncertainty.

contradictions.description: The central claim is improved predictive accuracy, but success and falsification are defined by whether measured conductivity is lower than the conventional model's prediction rather than by whether the ML model has lower prediction error on matched held-out samples. A signed difference from the conventional prediction does not establish greater accuracy and could instead reflect bias in either model.
